EC2 provides scalable cloud servers for businesses running applications and workloads, while Bedrock enables developers to access artificial intelligence models and build generative AI applications.
The distinction allows AWS to maintain access for customers requiring flexible computing resources despite the substantial long-term infrastructure commitments.
The comments highlight the growing importance of securing cloud capacity as technology companies compete to expand their AI capabilities.
They also underscore the capital-intensive nature of the AI infrastructure expansion, with major cloud providers committing substantial resources ahead of anticipated customer demand.

title: US Justice Dept sues to block possible Alaska election of Democrat to Senate
full_text:
By Jan Wolfe
Oct 23 (Reuters) - The Trump administration has sued Alaska to preemptively block the state from certifying the results of its US Senate race if the Republican incumbent candidate loses narrowly, saying voters could be confused because two Republicans on the ballot have almost identical names.
The Department of Justice’s lawsuit, filed in federal court in Anchorage on Thursday, signals the willingness of President Donald Trump’s administration to contest the results of the November 3 midterm elections that will decide control of the US Congress, where his fellow Republicans narrowly control both chambers.
The administration has taken an increasingly aggressive approach to election oversight, pressing states for voter-registration data and arguing that stricter measures are needed to ensure public confidence in the vote. Critics, including Democratic and some Republican election officials, view the moves as federal overreach.
Control of the Senate could come down to Alaska, where incumbent Republican Dan S. Sullivan is running a close race against Democrat Mary Peltola.
The suit, which names the state and local election officials as defendants, takes issue with the presence of another contender in the race, another Republican named Dan J. Sullivan Jr, alleging he is running "with the intention of misleading supporters of Senator Sullivan into voting for him."
The DOJ asks a judge to block the certification of an outcome "that may be impacted by voter confusion," so that there can be "an investigation to determine whether votes cast for Daniel J. Sullivan were meant to be cast for Senator Sullivan."
Trump told reporters on Friday that he supported the lawsuit, saying "I’m the one that said do it."
A DOJ spokesperson said in a statement that the agency is taking "necessary steps to ensure that this frivolous candidacy does not undermine the integrity of Alaska’s election or the will of its voters.”
Election officials around the country have told Reuters they are preparing for potential federal interference in the elections, including legal challenges and disputes over voting that could disrupt certification of the results.
Trump has a long history of challenging election outcomes and encouraging supporters to contest results he views as unfavorable.
Alaska’s other US senator, Senator Lisa Murkowski from Trump’s Republican Party, said on Friday the Justice Department "should never have filed this lawsuit."
Election law experts said the lawsuit has no merit and seeks relief not allowed under federal law.
"In short, like many Department letters over the last few years, it is designed to win the press release rather than the litigation," wrote Notre Dame law professor Derek Muller in a blog post, adding that "the legal argument is one of the worst ones I’ve ever seen."
Trump’s administration "has absolutely no authority to tell Alaska when or how to certify the results of its Senate election," said David Becker of the Center for Election Innovation and Research, a nonpartisan group that advises election officials, adding that "this issue has already been fully litigated by Alaska’s courts."
The unelected Sullivan, a former US Forest Service worker and elementary school teacher, filed to run as a candidate on May 29, seeking to unseat Dan S. Sullivan and "put Alaska first," according to his campaign website, which advertised "Dan Sullivan Challenges Dan Sullivan for US Senate Seat."
Dan J. Sullivan has denied in interviews with US news outlets that his aim is to cause confusion or divert votes from Dan S. Sullivan.
The Alaska Supreme Court in June permitted the challenger Sullivan to appear on the ballot. He will appear without a party designation next to his name, while the senator will be listed as the Republican incumbent.
Peltola, the Democratic candidate, told MS NOW on Friday that because of how the candidates are displayed on the ballot "there just isn’t much room for confusion." The lawsuit is "sending a message that Dan Sullivan does not believe that Alaskans are sophisticated enough to know exactly who they’re voting for," she added.
Trump’s approval rating has fallen to a record low, hit by rising diesel and gasoline prices during the Iran war, which has proven deeply unpopular with voters.
Public opinion polls suggest Republicans may lose control of one or both chambers of Congress, which would likely limit Trump’s ability to enact some of his policy agenda in the final two years of his presidency.

title: Boeing 777 freighter output halted for two months over supplier row - Reuters
full_text:

Investing.com -- Boeing (NYSE) has suspended production of its 777 freighter for nearly two months following a dispute with a key parts supplier, Reuters reported Friday exclusively, citing company workers and court documents.
The disruption has also affected production of Boeing’s 767 aircraft, including commercial freighters and KC-46 aerial refuelling tankers used by the U.S. military.
The dispute centres on Florida-based supplier Vaero, which allegedly stopped delivering trailing-edge rib kits used in aircraft wing assembly.
According to an August legal complaint reviewed by Reuters, Boeing identified Vaero as the sole supplier of the critical component, describing the parts as essential to maintaining production.
The interruption was costing the aerospace manufacturer as much as $6.5 million daily, according to the complaint.
Although the companies settled in late September, production of the 777 freighter has not resumed, three Boeing workers familiar with the situation told Reuters.
Some components have since arrived for the 767 programme, allowing limited progress on affected aircraft.
Meanwhile, Boeing is reportedly working to bring manufacturing of the trailing-edge rib kits in-house to reduce its dependence on the supplier.
The disruption has forced the company to remove two partially assembled 777 freighters from its final assembly line in Everett, Washington.
One of those aircraft was identified through aviation consultancy IBA data as destined for FedEx (NYSE).
Boeing’s next-generation 777X programme has not been affected because it uses composite wings rather than the components involved in the dispute.
The company has delivered 21 777 freighters so far this year, according to its published delivery figures.
Several additional aircraft whose wings were assembled before the supply interruption could still be delivered before the end of 2026.
The production setback comes as Boeing faces continued pressure to stabilise manufacturing operations and maintain deliveries across its commercial and defence programmes.
Neither Boeing nor Vaero provided comments to Reuters, while FedEx also did not respond to requests for comment.

title: U.S. repeatedly asked Musk to restrict or expand Starlink access, Reuters says
full_text:
Investing.com -- Successive U.S. administrations have asked Elon Musk’s SpaceX to alter Starlink access in several countries, Reuters reported Friday exclusively.
Citing six former senior U.S. officials, Reuters reported that both the Biden and Trump administrations sought changes to Starlink coverage to support allies and disrupt communications used by adversaries.
Under former President Joe Biden, officials requested restrictions on terminals allegedly used by Iran-backed groups, including Hezbollah in Lebanon and the Houthis in Yemen.
Intelligence shared with SpaceX indicated that militants had obtained Starlink equipment through intermediaries, prompting requests to identify and deactivate specific terminals.
At least some terminals were subsequently disabled, according to former officials familiar with the discussions.
Meanwhile, Washington sought expanded Starlink access in Ukraine following Russia’s 2022 invasion and in Iran during anti-government protests that year.
President Donald Trump’s administration reportedly pursued similar arrangements following U.S.-Israeli strikes against Iran in 2025 and 2026, although activation of the terminals has not been publicly confirmed.
The disclosures follow recent restrictions on Ukraine’s Starshield military satellite service, which Kyiv says have disrupted drone operations and battlefield communications.
Reuters previously reported that the order to reduce Starshield speeds originated inside the White House.
Musk has maintained that Starshield systems are controlled by the U.S. government, with operational restrictions ultimately determined by military authorities and the president.
Trump said Friday he would contact Musk if necessary to resolve Ukraine’s communications problems.
The controversy has intensified concerns among European officials about dependence on SpaceX infrastructure for critical military capabilities.
Ukraine currently lacks a comparable alternative to Starlink for frontline communications and drone operations.
Democratic lawmaker Jason Crow has also called for greater transparency over the restrictions, questioning the national security implications of relying heavily on private companies.
SpaceX did not respond to Reuters’ requests for comment.

Investing.com -- SpaceX’s proposed $40 billion AI financing deal has hit obstacles amid credit market volatility and rising borrowing costs, Bloomberg reported exclusively, citing people familiar with the matter.

Goldman Sachs (NYSE) is leading discussions with investors headed by Apollo Global Management (NYSE), according to the report.

Earlier discussions placed yields on a subordinated portion of the debt around the mid-8% range, although worsening market conditions have prompted renewed pricing negotiations.
The proposed financing would involve three tranches of privately placed bonds, including a subordinated portion estimated at $25 billion to $30 billion.
Other tranches would total approximately $10 billion and up to $5 billion, according to Bloomberg.
The structure follows an earlier financing arrangement involving Elon Musk’s AI startup xAI that failed to achieve its intended accounting treatment.
SpaceX subsequently recognised approximately $13 billion in debt after auditors determined the arrangement did not qualify as a completed sale-leaseback transaction.
The latest financing discussions follow SpaceX’s third-quarter results, which showed its AI business turning profitable for the first time.
The company’s Memphis data centres have increasingly generated revenue by supplying computing capacity to external AI developers and major technology companies.
SpaceX executives have indicated that additional borrowing will be necessary to support expansion while maintaining investment-grade credit ratings.
The proposed deal also follows Apollo’s involvement in a major AI chip financing arrangement involving Anthropic and Broadcom (NASDAQ).

The Basel-based company submitted its registration documents to the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission on Friday, outlining plans to list on the Nasdaq Global Market under the ticker WWB.
Founded in 2024, Windward is developing antibody-based treatments targeting severe asthma, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and inflammatory skin conditions.
Its drug pipeline includes a monoclonal antibody undergoing advanced clinical trials for respiratory diseases and a bispecific antibody in early-stage testing for inflammatory conditions, including eczema.
The company reported a net loss of $42.6 million for the six months ended June 30, 2026, compared with a $22.8 million loss during the corresponding period last year.
Windward generated no revenue in either period as it continued investing in clinical development.
The biotechnology firm has raised approximately $365 million in equity financing, including a $165 million funding round completed in May.

title: France’s luxury stores board up windows ahead of fresh protests
full_text:
By Alessandro Parodi
PARIS, Oct 24 (Reuters) - Luxury boutiques in France boarded up their normally glitzy windows and added guards ahead of fresh protests on Saturday, with some planning to stay closed after rioters looted shops across the country last weekend.
France, the most visited country in the world, draws large numbers of overseas shoppers seeking Chanel handbags and Hermes scarves, an important source of revenue for brands facing slowing demand.
But some decided staying open was too risky after last week’s events, when rioters smashed and looted hundreds of shops in Paris, Marseille and Bordeaux.
A Rolex retailer and a De Beers store near the capital’s famous Place Vendome will remain closed on Saturday, staff said, while managers at stores including Richemont-owned IWC said they would decide whether to close early depending on the intensity of the protests.
Groups including France’s main student union UNEF and the Yellow Vest group, which emerged as a potent anti-establishment movement in 2018, plan to march through central Paris later on Saturday to protest against high living costs and cuts to public services.
NOT IN THE MOOD
Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said on Friday that his ministry would deploy 70,000 police officers, backed by specialist units, to prevent the violence that occurred last week.
But staff at LVMH brands Louis Vuitton, Dior and Bulgari said they weren’t taking any chances and security at their stores near Place Vendome had been increased for the day. Additional private security to supplement the police presence in the neighbourhood is also planned.
Nearby department store Printemps also increased its security staff, carried out safety repairs and added security measures to reinforce shop windows and entrances, a spokesperson for the store said.
Hermes finance chief Eric du Halgouet said this week the company had increased security measures at its French stores, adding it was too early to say how much impact recent events would have on business.
The image-conscious industry can ill afford further negative publicity. Consumer sentiment is gloomy worldwide and tourism is slowing as a result of the Iran war — contributing to disappointing quarterly reports at LVMH, Hermes and Kering this month.
Lidiya Shevchenko, a sales assistant at a Graziella Braccialini store, said she doubted many people would be looking to visit stores anyway during the protests.
"I suppose the mood is just as important when it comes to shopping," Shevchenko said.
One tourist who has already been put off is Cambodian Jerry Lay, who purchased several items from Louis Vuitton on the Champs-Élysées earlier this week.
"We do enjoy shopping in France, but after experiencing the protest (last Saturday), I’d say it’s 50/50 whether I would consider coming back next time," Lay said.

full_text:

By Matt Spetalnick
WASHINGTON, Oct 24 (Reuters) - Foreign policy is rarely the deciding factor in US midterm elections, when economic considerations usually drive voters’ choices.
But this time, with Donald Trump’s war against Iran and his sweeping tariff campaign pushing up costs for Americans, a president’s approach to world affairs has itself become a pocketbook issue.
As the November 3 elections approach, there are growing signs that voters are drawing that connection directly, creating a major liability for Trump and his fellow Republicans and imperiling their control of Congress.
Those include a Reuters/Ipsos poll earlier this month showing some 78% of Americans blame Trump’s policies for rising prices that are outpacing their earnings.
Not since 2006, when President George W. Bush’s Republicans lost both legislative chambers while he was mired in the unpopular Iraq war, has a US leader’s handling of international events appeared so central to shaping the midterms outcome.
The political backlash for Trump could be even bigger, with opinion polls showing that voters feel the economic pain from high gas prices and rising grocery bills in a way that they didn’t two decades ago.
“The bottom line is people are experiencing the impact of Trump’s war and other policies,” said Christopher Preble, a senior fellow at the Stimson Center think tank in Washington. “Now voters have a chance to register their discontent with how he’s dealing with all this.”
POLITICS DRIVING FOREIGN POLICY
With Trump’s approval ratings touching historic lows, he has left little doubt, despite his public claims to the contrary, that he sees the straight line voters are drawing between his foreign policy and their cost of living.
That has prompted some controversial policy moves in the run-up to the elections.
Chief among them was Trump’s lifting of sanctions on Russian diesel exports aimed at bringing down fuel prices, a step his critics, including some fellow Republicans, say reinforces the impression that he is increasingly siding with Moscow in its war in Ukraine.
He has also pressed Kyiv to halt strikes on Russian refineries as he tries to shift the blame for high US gasoline prices despite experts saying the surge in energy costs is mainly the result of the war he launched alongside Israel against Iran nearly eight months ago.
At the same time, he has promised not to order any new attack on Iran before the midterms, though the US and Israel are widely reported to be preparing for a possible major escalation after the elections.
Polls have shown that most voters oppose the war initiated by Trump, who had campaigned on avoiding new foreign interventions. He has insisted Americans should accept temporarily higher gas prices so that he can block Iran from developing a nuclear weapon.
Iran says its nuclear program is for civilian purposes. The UN nuclear watchdog and US intelligence community have assessed that Tehran shuttered a nuclear weapons development program in 2003.
Some Republican candidates have distanced themselves from Trump on matters ranging from the conflict in the Middle East to the trade war with Canada and his pressure campaign against Ukraine.
For its part, Iran has sought to keep oil prices high and hurt Trump in the midterms by deploying new tactics to target ships transiting the Strait of Hormuz and deliberately prolonging the diplomatic stalemate, senior Iranian officials have told Reuters.
Defending the administration’s approach, White House spokesman Matt Middleton said: "President Trump has always been clear about temporary market disruptions as a result of the conflict in Iran, but the contrast between President Trump’s economic record and Democrats’ ruinous alternative is clear."
‘IT’S THE ECONOMY, STUPID’
Midterm elections historically have been seen as a referendum on the performance of the incumbent in the White House.
And in one election after another in recent decades, the conventional wisdom has been that economic concerns - “it’s the economy, stupid,” as the Clinton-era adage goes - dominate voters’ choices.
Opinion polls for this year’s midterms, including the Reuters/Ipsos survey, show that while voters rank foreign policy low on their list of priorities, it is clear that most Americans see some of Trump’s signature moves on the world stage, such as the Iran war and tariffs, feeding into their higher costs.
Other polls have shown that a majority of Americans have also soured more broadly on Trump’s international approach.
The Chicago Council on Global Affairs said its latest nationwide survey “finds that most Americans believe the Trump administration’s foreign policy actions have negatively impacted America’s global standing and hurt national and household economic conditions.”
Since returning to the White House last year, Trump has shaken up the rules-based global order that Washington helped create from the ashes of World War Two while his relations with allies have steadily worsened and the limits of US power have been increasingly exposed, analysts say.
LEGISLATIVE BALANCE OF POWER IN PLAY
Against this backdrop, Democrats are widely projected to gain control of the House of Representatives in the midterms, with the Senate also seen as increasingly in play.
For Republicans, losing either chamber could complicate Trump’s agenda in the last two years of his second term.
But even with a shift in the balance of power on Capitol Hill on November 3, lawmakers will have a hard time reining in Trump’s capacity to pursue foreign policy as he sees fit.
Once the ballots are counted, a big question will be whether Trump will feel either restricted or emboldened on the world stage as he enters what is traditionally considered a lame-duck phase - when a president is barred from running again and no longer faces electoral consequences for decisions made.
“For many presidents who feel politically constrained (at home), foreign policy is the area where they are able to act with relative freedom,” said Jon Alterman of the Center for Strategic and International Studies think tank in Washington.
Analysts say Trump’s handling of adversaries such as Iran, Russia, China and even Cuba or his approach to allies across the globe could go either way -- or he could simply lose interest and double down on his string of construction projects, such as the White House ballroom.

By Eduardo Baptista
BEIJING, Oct 24 (Reuters) - Moonshot AI has reduced the cyber-offensive capabilities of its newest model, the Chinese startup said on Saturday, as fears grow that increasingly autonomous AI could turbocharge hacking.
Beijing-based Moonshot announced the curbs while introducing Kimi K3.1 Pro, which it describes as its most capable 3-trillion-parameter-class open-weight model. The company plans to publish the model’s weights — files allowing outside developers to run and modify it on their own systems — by November 4.
Moonshot said it removed cyber-related data from the training corpus and reinforcement-learning environments used to develop the model, while retaining general coding skills.
"We aim not to release open weights that would extend the absolute frontier of cyber capability," the company said.
Governments, technology companies and security researchers are growing increasingly concerned that AI could make sophisticated hacking easier and cheaper. Models that can write code, operate software tools and complete long, multi-step tasks may help users identify weaknesses in programs and automate parts of cyberattacks.
China proposed export controls last week that would ban exports of AI-driven malware-generation and mutation technology and restrict AI-assisted vulnerability-discovery tools. The draft measures, which remain open for public comment, cite the risk that such capabilities could be used against critical infrastructure, defence-industrial and core government systems, or to bypass security protections.
Moonshot said open-weight models can improve security by helping more organisations inspect and secure their own software, including older systems that receive little attention.
Unlike proprietary, closed-weight AI systems, however, open-weight releases make central oversight more difficult. Once the files are widely distributed, the original developer has less ability to restrict access, monitor use or update safeguards than with a hosted service.
K3.1 Pro scored 81.0% on its internal cyber benchmark, compared with 90.5% for a similar version without the risk-reduction measures, the company said. The test involved finding and exploiting software vulnerabilities in a controlled environment. Moonshot said the comparison showed that filtering cyber-related data reduced the model’s offensive cyber performance, although it still outperformed its predecessor. The results have not been independently verified.
K3.1 Pro has a 1-million-token context window, allowing it to process very large amounts of text at once. Moonshot also released a faster version, K3.1 Pro Highspeed, which it said runs at two to three times the speed of the standard model.

title: As winter nears, heating oil emerges as hurdle for Republicans in US Senate races
full_text:
By Tim McLaughlin, Nichola Groom, Timothy Gardner and Leah Douglas
KINGSTON, New Hampshire, Oct 24 (Reuters) - Eighty-year-old Rick Russman of New Hampshire spent five decades as a Republican. This year, as his state braces for a winter of soaring heating oil costs, he will vote for Democrat Chris Pappas in one of the country’s most closely watched Senate races.
For Russman, a resident of Kingston, the situation has become so dire that he will rely on a wood stove to help heat his home this winter rather than on heating oil alone. "Fuel that costs more than $6 a gallon is a huge expense," he said.
High heating oil prices are a potent issue in northern states that depend on the fuel like Maine, New Hampshire and Alaska, which have competitive Senate races on November 3 that could determine whether Trump’s fellow Republicans maintain control of Congress, according to Reuters interviews with 15 voters, candidates and strategists.
Democratic candidates have sought to tie the higher costs to Trump’s war with Iran, which has disrupted global diesel supplies. The shortage drove prices for diesel, which is similar to heating oil, to a record high above $6.50 a gallon, making groceries and consumer staples more expensive.
Reuters was first to report this week that the US Energy Department released heating oil from reserves in the Northeast.
When asked about criticism that Trump’s policies have led to soaring heating oil costs that could make Republicans vulnerable, the White House pointed to that fuel release, a move an analyst said was unlikely to affect prices.
Heating oil prices have climbed above $6 per gallon nationally, up from about $3.50 a year ago, according to the Energy Information Administration.
The costs are a headwind for Republicans, said Lance Dutson, a Republican strategist in Maine. "The party in power is held responsible for things like that, and it’s so clearly Trump’s fault because of this Iran war."
Nearly 80% of Americans blame Trump policies for higher costs including energy, according to an October Reuters/Ipsos poll.
In New Hampshire, where 43% of residents use heating oil, Pappas said energy dominates voters’ concerns as he challenges Republican John Sununu.
"Energy costs and heating oil prices are the beginning and end of every conversation I’m having on the campaign trail," Pappas said.
Sununu’s campaign did not respond to several requests for comment.
ALASKA EVEN HIGHER
In Alaska, where roughly 30% of residents rely on heating oil, the issue has surfaced in the Senate race between Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan and Democrat Mary Peltola, who has campaigned on lowering energy costs.
In remote Alaska communities, fuel is often shipped long distances. Diesel also generates electricity and powers transportation, pushing up the cost of goods and services.
In the Yukon River community of St. Mary’s, Mayor Sven Paukan said heating fuel has risen to about $10 per gallon, roughly $2 more than last year.
"It’s pretty difficult to heat homes nowadays," Paukan said.
Sullivan said he supports a "temporary pause of American diesel exports," a policy Trump has considered. A Peltola spokesperson said the Iran war had helped drive up heating fuel, gasoline and grocery costs in Alaska.
Sullivan has said he supports the war but that it should end soon, and this week he encouraged Alaska fishermen to apply for a new $8 billion Trump administration program to offset diesel costs for farmers.
Suzanne Downing, former communications director for the Alaska Republican Party, said heating oil is a concern for Republicans. "Many people in Fairbanks ... pay more in the wintertime for their fuel bill than they do for their mortgage," she said. "The Iran war is being blamed for this."
MAINE ’DOUBLE WHAMMY’
In Maine, where 54% of homes use heating oil, rising fuel costs have featured in the Senate race between Republican incumbent Susan Collins and Democrat Troy Jackson.
The costs are even higher for fishermen and farmers who use diesel to power their motors and warm homes with oil. "For them, it really is a double whammy," said Mark Brewer, chair of the political science department at the University of Maine.
"Folks who probably have the lowest incomes are the ones who are facing the highest energy costs," said Scott Thistle, spokesperson for MaineHousing, the public housing authority, adding older housing stock and mobile homes are costlier to heat.
Gerry Cushman, a fifth-generation lobsterman from Port Clyde, said fishermen were already facing fluctuating prices for their catches.
But Cushman said he plans to support Collins, the Republican, arguing that her seniority and influence outweigh voters’ frustrations.
"If you’re a senior senator and you’re head of (Senate Committee on Appropriations), you can get more done than a freshman senator,” he said.
Collins said after initially supporting the war she has voted several times to bring it to an end. She also pushed the US government to speed the release of $38 million for Maine from the $4 billion federal Low Income Home Energy Assistance Program and urged Trump to tap the heating oil reserve.
That’s not enough for Maine lobsterman Dave Cousens of South Thomaston, who plans to vote for Jackson. Cousens blamed high energy costs on Trump’s Iran war and said he will be forced to forgo a Florida vacation.
"He picked a fight with the wrong country, and we’re all paying for it."

title: Five takeaways from Trump’s midterm campaign rallies
full_text:
By Steve Holland, Bo Erickson, Nandita Bose and Jacob Bogage
Oct 24 (Reuters) - President Donald Trump is in the midst of a nationwide campaign blitz ahead of the November midterm elections, holding near-daily rallies to boost turnout for Republicans who are fighting to keep control of Congress.
In his 90-minute stump speeches, Trump defends his economic policies, boasts about crowd size, mocks protesters and has even admired a fellow Republican’s buttocks.
Here are five takeaways from Reuters coverage of the president’s appearances, staged mostly in Republican-friendly areas across the country:
TRUMP’S ECONOMIC PITCH COLLIDES WITH VOTER REALITY
At the start of the month, Trump said he had done a “bad job” explaining his economic record. He has tried to remedy that at his rallies, pointing to a record-low poverty rate, low unemployment, record highs in the stock market and cheaper prices for some food items.
But his sales pitch is colliding with voters’ concerns about how much they are spending on gas, groceries and other everyday expenses.
Consumer prices accelerated in September as the cost of gasoline surged. The nationwide average price of gas is $4.27 per gallon ($1.13 per litre), nearly 40% higher than a year ago, according to AAA. Trump has repeatedly promised that gas prices will fall once the Iran war ends.
The disconnect was evident outside Trump’s rally in rural Kansas, where Chester Daniel, a 90-year-old military veteran and Trump supporter, said the economy has “a long way to go” to help working people.
“Prices? Too high! We will never go back to what they were when this all started, but they need to come way down," Daniel said. "I don’t know how these young people make a living for their family."
RALLY MAP SHOWS REPUBLICANS PLAYING DEFENSE
Trump’s travel map signals just how difficult it will be for Republicans to retain control of Congress, with the president forced to play defense deep in conservative territory.
Trump has traveled twice to Texas for Republican Senate nominee Ken Paxton, campaigned for Republican Senate incumbent Roger Marshall in Kansas and made two stops in Ohio for Senator Jon Husted. Trump also rallied for Republicans in competitive races in Alaska, Iowa, Montana and South Carolina. He is set to visit Mississippi on Monday.
Those are places Republicans are accustomed to winning easily, not battlegrounds where Trump would spend time during the crucial final weeks before an election.
Paxton narrowly trails Democrat James Talarico in polls, while Marshall faces a serious challenge from Democrat Adam Hamilton in a state that has not elected a Democratic senator in nearly a century. Husted trails former Democratic Senator Sherrod Brown in polls in Ohio, and Republican Senate hopeful Ashley Hinson is in a close race against Democrat Josh Turek in Iowa.
Notably absent from Trump’s travels so far with less than two weeks until Election Day: Michigan, Maine, Minnesota and New Hampshire – also home to tight Senate races. He is soon poised to hit some of those locations. He is scheduled travel to Michigan on Sunday and has said he also plans to go to Maine.
TRUMP’S BOASTS ABOUT BIG CROWDS MEET UNEVEN REALITY
Trump has made crowd sizes a recurring theme of his midterm rallies, portraying packed arenas and thousands of people he says are stranded outside as evidence of his persisting popularity.
But actual turnout on the campaign trail in recent weeks has been uneven. Some rallies have drawn capacity crowds but have shown little sign of the overflow Trump described. At others, large sections of seats remained empty even in modest-sized venues.
"I’m doing these every night, and no matter where I go, it’s the same thing. It’s massive crowds," Trump said at a rally in North Carolina on Tuesday. "We have big screens outside. Thousands and thousands of people. There’s something going on that’s very special."
The venue was filled to capacity, but there were no signs of crowds outside waiting to get in or watching on screens.
At an October 7 rally in San Antonio, Texas, Trump said lines stretched two miles outside the arena even as sizable sections inside remained empty.
Crowd sizes are not always an accurate measure of political support, but Trump has pointed to them as a sign of strength even as his approval rating has fallen to 31%, the lowest of either of his presidential terms, according to a Reuters/Ipsos poll released on Monday.
Trump is not on the ballot on November 3. For Republican candidates, the question is whether the enthusiasm he generates among his supporters can translate into votes for them.
FRANCE BECOMES A ’BETE NOIRE’ FOR MIDTERMS
Trump has often used French President Emmanuel Macron as a foil in his campaign stump speeches, claiming he strong-armed Macron into raising prescription drug prices in France by threatening tariffs on a popular French export, champagne, and other goods.
But in the last week or so Trump has seized on another narrative about France, casting its violent unrest of recent weeks as a warning of what he says could happen in the US if Democrats win in the midterms. Trump has blamed the unrest on migrants and Muslims, following a familiar playbook that has featured in his politics for more than a decade.
“What the hell happened to France?” Trump told a crowd in a livestock competition arena in Clemson, South Carolina, on Wednesday.
Notably, the French protests have taken a larger role in Trump’s recent speeches than two other major foreign policy headaches he has been unable to resolve: Russia’s invasion of Ukraine and his war against Iran.
“They’ll end one way or another,” Trump said of the two conflicts at his Clemson rally. He did not elaborate on how they might end, but complained that he was not awarded the Nobel Peace Prize for his work to resolve conflicts around the world.
TRUMP PUTS THE BODY IN BODY POLITIC
Trump has long had a fixation on the human physique that stretches beyond the body politic.
This campaign season, Trump has given particular attention to Husted, a 59-year-old former college football player for the University of Dayton.
At rallies in Ohio, Kentucky and North Carolina, Trump marveled at Husted’s physique, at one point saying his backside is “like a pile of muscle.”
“Then I looked at his legs, and I said, ‘Man, his feet are big.’ Then I looked at his shoulders, and I tapped him on the shoulder, and it actually hurt my hand. It was like a piece of steel. I said, ‘This guy’s a monster,’” Trump said.
Trump had similar praise on Friday for Robert F. Kennedy Jr., his secretary of health and human services, telling a campaign rally in Florida that the 72-year-old "has the body of a 30-year-old."
Such riffs are familiar terrain for Trump. At the close of his 2024 campaign, he used a Pennsylvania rally speech to tell a crude story about PGA legend Arnold Palmer’s prowess beyond his golf game. Trump’s focus over the years on people’s physical attributes has also included mocking the weight and looks of his opponents.
Trump finds even some of his friends lacking in fashion sense, including the rumpled Paxton.
"Some may not like the way he dresses," Trump said about him at the Republicans’ midterm convention in Dallas in mid-September, adding: "I don’t."
That has not stopped Trump from campaigning for Paxton, however. He returns to Texas on Tuesday for two more campaign rallies.

title: Divided over Israel, Detroit Democrats unite on rising costs for midterm elections
full_text:
By Heather Schlitz
DETROIT, Oct 24 (Reuters) - It was her son’s eighth birthday, but Dayna Broadnax could not afford a present.
Broadnax, a 42-year-old single mother of four in Detroit, said soaring gas and grocery prices left little money to pay the bills, let alone buy gifts or throw a birthday party.
“It’s hard to tell your kids that you don’t have the funds right now to buy them a $3 bag of Skittles,” she said while watching her sons practice with a free basketball team at St. Suzanne Community Resource Center.
Ahead of the November 3 midterm elections, Broadnax’s concerns are widely shared in Detroit. Jewish, Muslim and Black voters interviewed by Reuters often put affordability ahead of disputes over Israel and Gaza, even as many expressed reservations about Democratic US Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed.
El-Sayed, who could make history as the first Muslim US senator, faces former congressman Mike Rogers in a competitive race that could help determine control of the Senate. A RealClearPolitics average gives El-Sayed a two-point lead – 48% to 46%.
Broadnax has yet to decide who to support, saying she will vote for the candidate most focused on lowering costs.
She sometimes skips meals so her children can eat and chooses which bills to pay after gas eats up at least $50 of the $150 she makes on a typical day driving for Lyft.
“Being a single mom, trying to take care of four boys out here in America now is too hard,” she said. “Whatever candidate whose main focus is affordability – that’s who I’m going with.”
But El-Sayed faces resistance from some voters who would ordinarily be inclined to support a Democrat, particularly over Israel.
“Both of the candidates have decided that this election is about Abdul,” said Matt Grossmann, a political science professor at Michigan State University. “He needs to win over voters that would normally support the Democratic candidate and are upset with President Trump but might have reservations about him – personal or policy reservations.”
El-Sayed’s challenge is not only keeping uneasy Democrats from voting for Rogers, but getting them to vote at all. Some voters told Reuters that opposing Trump made backing Rogers difficult, while concerns about El-Sayed led others to consider sitting out the race.
JEWISH VOTERS’ RESERVATIONS
Most Jewish voters in Detroit traditionally vote Democratic, but some have deep reservations about El-Sayed over his views on Israel, particularly his response to a March attack on a suburban synagogue. After a man rammed his truck into Temple Israel while more than 100 children were inside, El-Sayed drew backlash when he said “hurt people hurt people" in reference to the attacker.
Though El-Sayed later apologized for the comment, he has continued to draw heavy criticism from a community shaken by the attack.
Rabbi Aaron Starr of Congregation Shaarey Zedek said some Jewish men now cover their heads with baseball caps instead of yarmulkes because they fear being targeted if identified as Jews. Starr’s synagogue spends twice as much on security measures for its sprawling campus following the attack.
Starr and a group of Jewish clergy launched a petition calling for the Democratic Party to agree to a set of “non-negotiable” principles, including acknowledging Israel’s right to exist and Jewish sovereignty in Israel. El-Sayed has not signed the petition or communicated with the group, Starr said. He said he would not vote for the Democratic nominee.
“He is hyper-focused on Israel and American supporters of the state of Israel and seemed to be placing an awful lot of blame on Israel for America’s problems,” Starr said in his study, where “hurt people help people” yard signs leaned against a wall beside shelves of religious texts.
El-Sayed briefly campaigned with Hasan Piker, a left-wing streamer who has drawn criticism over comments about Israel and American Jews. The association has troubled some voters, while others remain more focused on the cost of living.
“I don’t love the fact that he campaigned with Hasan Piker during the primary,” said Alicia Chandler, a 47-year-old Jewish Detroit resident and former supporter of El-Sayed’s Democratic primary opponent Haley Stevens. “But it cost me almost $100 to fill my car with gas yesterday.”
El-Sayed has repeatedly pledged to protect Jewish people from antisemitism, saying in an August speech after winning the Democratic primary that his commitment to Jewish safety was “the same commitment that I have to the safety of my own daughters.”
GAZA AND THE POCKETBOOK
In 2024, frustration with the Biden-Harris administration’s support for Israel’s war in Gaza drove many Arab American and Muslim voters in Michigan away from the Democratic ticket, with some backing the Republican Trump or third-party candidates and others choosing not to vote.
At Shibam Coffee, a Yemeni coffeehouse in the Arab-majority city of Dearborn, volunteers wearing “Abdul for Senate” shirts gathered over cardamom coffee, honeycomb bread and sambusas before heading out to canvass. The cafe is popular with young Arab Americans, many of whom now support El-Sayed.
Sumayah Dhalai, a 22-year-old senior at Wayne State University who plans to vote for El-Sayed, liked his policy position opposing funding for the Israeli government but said her fears about finding a job and affording rent and groceries were a bigger factor in deciding who to vote for.
“The overwhelming majority of us are very scared about graduating because everybody’s telling us that everything sucks,” Dhalai said. “As much as I want to say I’m out here fighting for world peace, I have to ensure my own ability to succeed before I can then turn to focus on everybody else’s.”
While parts of Detroit have benefited from new investment, others have not, including the neighborhood housing St. Suzanne Community Resource Center, where the median household income is just $36,525 and roughly half the children live in poverty, according to US Census data.
“The financial stress is continual,” said Steve Wasko, the director of the center where Broadnax’s sons play basketball. “Being able to pay your rent, afford your light bill, pay your mortgage, or pay to have your furnace working sufficiently – these are the most common requests that come through the door."

By Jonathan Allen
Oct 24 (Reuters) - Kamala Harris is returning to the campaign trail to help Democrats in some of the tightest US midterm races, putting the former vice president back before voters as she weighs whether to make a third run for the presidency in 2028.
The Democratic Party’s unsuccessful 2024 standard-bearer has made relatively few public appearances this year. But with her party trying to break the Republican hold on Congress on November 3, Harris is rallying in Georgia, Mississippi, Nevada, New Hampshire and Wisconsin, a return likely to renew questions about her political future as a crowded field of potential 2028 contenders takes shape.
Harris kicked off her tour in Las Vegas on Tuesday with a new stump speech attacking what she described as the cruelty of President Donald Trump, mixed with the aspirational aphorisms that have long been her calling card as the first Black and Asian person and first woman to become vice president.
She spoke to scores of Culinary Workers Union members alongside gubernatorial candidate Aaron Ford, Nevada’s first Black attorney general, who she said would be the "first Black governor west of the Mississippi."
"We got a serious fight in front of us," Harris said. "We are witnessing pure brutality come out of what is undoubtedly the most corrupt, callous and incompetent presidential administration."
Like Trump, who is jetting around the country for Republican candidates, Harris is not broadly popular among voters. A Reuters/Ipsos opinion poll in June showed 39% of Americans viewed her favorably, but the figures were starkly partisan: 82% of Democrats viewed her favorably, compared to 7% of Republicans and 33% of independents.
"At the end of a campaign, you bring out your heavy hitters," said Elaine Kamarck, a senior fellow at the Brookings Institution and a member of the Democratic National Committee. "That’s what’s going on here with her, and frankly with Trump."
The day after Las Vegas, Harris led chants of "Mississippi matters!" to a crowd supporting Scott Colom in the city of Columbus. Colom is seeking to become the first Democratic US senator elected in Mississippi since 1982, and polls show an unusually tight race with Republican Cindy Hyde-Smith.
Harris opened with advice she said she gives young people she mentors: "Never let someone else’s limited ability to see your capacity be a limitation on your ambition," she said. "Let me repeat that." And she did, louder than the first time, drawing cheers from the crowd.
UNDECIDED ON 2028
If Harris decides to run again for the White House in 2028, she would likely be among the most high-profile names in what is expected to be a crowded Democratic field.
But Harris also carries the baggage of past defeats: she lost the 2024 presidential election to Trump, and her first White House campaign ended before the 2020 Democratic nominating contests began.
A 2028 campaign would also force Harris to revisit the Democrats’ chaotic 2024 race, when then-President Joe Biden abruptly ended his reelection campaign over questions about his health and mental acuity and she replaced him as the nominee.
Harris has since called Biden’s decision to seek reelection "reckless" in her memoir "107 Days," a reference to the short campaign she inherited. This month, she offered her clearest criticism yet of his support for Israel’s war in Gaza, rebuking the Israeli government’s "horrific conduct" and saying the US should have "acted sooner and more forcefully."
"All these things will be relitigated," Kamarck said. "What happened to Biden? Did she know? Did she think he was losing it? And on and on and on."
Scott Ferson, a Democratic strategist and author of "How the Democrats Lost America," said the party has tended to give short shrift to candidates who have lost, though voters disillusioned with Trump may also view Harris in a new light.
"She has that kind of crossover appeal," Ferson said, "particularly with people who left in 2024 or stayed home." Her implicit message, he suggested, is "Do you regret staying home?"
This month, as she wrapped up an appearance on the "Baby, This Is Keke Palmer" video podcast, Palmer asked her if she would run again.
"Oh, girl, come on!" Harris said, laughing while gripping the hands of the Hollywood movie star. "I haven’t decided yet."
"But the midterms, the midterms, the midterms," Harris went on. "2028 don’t matter if we don’t do 2026 right."

Capital Economics Chief Europe Economist Andrew Kenningham wrote that although France appears headed toward an escalating fiscal crisis that will likely push government bond spreads higher, structural safeguards should keep the fallout largely confined to Paris’s sovereign debt market.
Echoing that view, Ismael García Puente, Deputy Director of Investment Strategy at Mapfre AM, said a full-blown financial crisis would require three conditions: -
A French government denying its fiscal reality, European partners willing to let that government collapse, and an absence of institutional crisis tools.
"None of these three conditions appears to be in place at the moment," García Puente said.
Why contagion risks are contained
French private-sector borrowing costs have risen far less than sovereign yields, allowing blue-chip corporates such as LVMH Moët Hennessy Louis Vuitton SE and Airbus SE to borrow at yields below those of the French state. Furthermore, French domestic banks hold only around 2% of total assets in domestic sovereign bonds - a fraction of the sovereign exposures held by lenders in Italy or Spain.
Unlike the fragmented policy environment of 2010-2012, the European Central Bank has established backstops, notably the Transmission Protection Instrument (TPI), to shield "innocent bystander" countries from unjustified yield spikes.
Broader euro area economies are not suffering from large external imbalances; major member states outside Greece are posting balanced current accounts or surpluses, with manageable private debt and stable real estate markets.
Political risk around single-currency fragmentation has ebbed, with leading French right-wing figure Marine Le Pen abandoning her euro-exit stance years ago and parallel currency proposals in Italy remaining off the table.
Kenningham cautioned, however, that an open political confrontation between a future French government and European Union authorities over deficit discipline could push
spreads toward 400 to 500 basis points - resembling Italy’s 2012 crisis - though he characterized this outcome as a tail risk.
Stronger bank balance sheets and market outlook
On the banking sector, Mapfre AM’s García Puente emphasized that European lenders are far better capitalized today and play a vital role in channeling government stimulus programs.
"At present, banks are more necessary than ever as a vehicle for financing all the stimulus plans," García Puente said. "Although their exposure to French debt may weigh on them in the short term, their fundamentals are solid and they are not a concern for us."

title: France dodges Moody’s downgrade amid protests and budget gridlock
full_text:
Investing.com - France dodged an immediate credit rating downgrade from Moody’s Ratings on Friday, offering temporary respite to a government grappling with soaring borrowing costs, parliamentary gridlock, and widespread civil unrest.
Moody’s affirmed the euro zone’s second-largest economy at Aa3 - seven notches above junk and on par with Britain - while maintaining a negative outlook.
"Slower growth and a higher deficit have pushed France’s debt burden somewhat higher than previously expected," Moody’s said, noting that surging bond yields and escalating social protests could hinder fiscal consolidation. The agency said its baseline assumes a deficit-reducing budget will eventually pass, "possibly by decree."
French Finance Minister Roland Lescure welcomed the decision, saying it reflected "the credibility of the budget the government has put forward in the 2027 finance bill."
Political paralysis and widening spreads
The reprieve follows weeks of intense bond market volatility. France’s 10-year yield touched 5.14% this week, its highest level since July 2002. The closely watched risk premium over benchmark German Bunds reached 178 basis points on Thursday, up from 85 basis points in early September and marking its widest gap in 15 years, according to Reuters.
Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu is attempting to steer an austerity package through a fractured parliament to narrow the deficit from 5.4% of GDP this year to 5% in 2027. However, the National Assembly rejected the revenue portion of the social security bill on Friday, underscoring the risk of a no-confidence vote ahead of the spring presidential election.
Unrest imperils consolidation
Street protests have compounded investor unease. After more than 500,000 demonstrators rallied against living costs last weekend - with riots triggering looting across several cities - authorities mobilized 70,000 police officers nationwide on Saturday to prevent further violence.
Moody’s assessment leaves France rated one notch higher than at S&P Global and Fitch, both of which downgraded the sovereign in late 2025. S&P is scheduled to review France on Nov. 27.

The alert from Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton came after Washington scaled back staffing at its mission in Saudi Arabia earlier this week in response to intensified attacks by Iran-allied Houthi forces.
Those attacks on one front of the nearly eight-month-old regional conflict triggered by the Iran war have coincided with a rise in attacks on commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz.
Earlier this month, sources told Reuters Iran was preparing a more forceful response if the United States resumes large-scale military attacks on its territory.
"Specifically, through various channels, we have received intelligence that Iran has substantially increased efforts to target US personnel," Clayton wrote to US Secretary of State Marco Rubio in a message dated October 23.
"The lethal plotting efforts by the Iranians against US citizens have reached advanced stages in both the Middle East and certain other countries," he added.
CIA Director John Ratcliffe was also copied in on the unclassified memo which was first reported by Axios.
The State Department on Wednesday ordered non-emergency government employees and their family members to leave US diplomatic missions in Saudi Arabia and planned to withdraw family members from a number of other missions in the region, US officials told Reuters.
On Saturday, the US State Department updated travel advisories for more than a dozen countries across the Gulf and Middle East, including Saudi Arabia, Qatar, the United Arab Emirates, Iraq and Israel, citing an increased threat from Iran-aligned Houthis.
"When it comes to our staffing at embassies, we constantly evaluate new information about the security environment," a US official said.
"The threat of Houthi attacks and of Iranian terror plots targeting US officials are informing our decisions on staffing adjustments for embassies on RO Status in the region," the official said.
The Restricted Operations Status provides the State Department more flexibility in personnel decisions without having to publicly announce a change in the status of a mission.

title: Ukraine says Starlink back to normal, Musk accuses Kyiv of violations
full_text:
By Yuliia Dysa
KYIV, Oct 24 (Reuters) - Ukraine said on Saturday the Starlink satellite system and its military version Starshield were now fully functional after over a week of restrictions that disrupted military operations and intensified tensions with the US.
Hours later, Elon Musk, who owns the systems, accused the Ukrainian military of violating Starlink’s terms. “Ukraine military violated Starlink terms of service and used it for offensive drone strikes to kill people. That loophole was closed last week”, he said on X. There were no immediate public comment from Ukrainian officials.
Problems with the systems came after US President Donald Trump announced a deal to buy Russian diesel while pressing Kyiv to stop striking Russian oil refineries.
Ukrainian officials said the restrictions, which capped operations at speeds of 160 kph (100 mph), hampered the military’s ability to intercept Russian attack drones and forced the cancellation of some operations.
"The main thing for today is that Starlink and Starshield have resumed operations at their pre-restriction speeds. The speeds are now at the level we need," President Volodymyr Zelenskiy said on the Telegram app.
According to Zelenskiy, the speeds started returning to normal overnight. Ukraine’s defence ministry said on Saturday the connection remained stable at over 400 kph.
Ukraine does not rely on the systems for long-range drone operations on Russian territory, including attacks on refineries.
But Starlink remains vital for frontline communications, and the deployment of Starshield-enabled medium-range attack drones has helped Ukraine gain the upper hand in several areas of the battlefield this year.
LIMITATIONS ORDER
The restrictions sparked outrage in Ukraine, particularly as they coincided with disruptions to allied warnings about incoming Russian missile attacks. Kyiv later said it continued to receive US intelligence.
Neither Musk nor the US government has acknowledged responsibility for restricting Starlink or Starshield in Ukraine. Both have said publicly that any such decision could only have been taken by the other.
Reuters has reported that the order to throttle Starshield came from inside the White House. Previously, US administrations had several times asked SpaceX to turn Starlink on or off in various countries, sources said.
On Friday, contradicting his previous statement that the services had been fully restored, Trump said that if problems persisted, he would "get it straightened out".

title: Violence flares in Paris after largely peaceful protests across France
full_text:
By Juliette Jabkhiro, Yann Tessier and Crispian Balmer
PARIS, Oct 24 (Reuters) - Hundreds of thousands of demonstrators marched in France on Saturday, with largely peaceful rallies giving way to clashes in Paris and Marseille as night fell despite a huge security operation aimed at preventing a repeat of last week’s unrest.
The Interior Ministry said 410,000 people took part in protests nationwide, though unions said the true figure was twice as high.
The main demonstration took place on the southeastern fringes of Paris, where at least 110,000 people turned out to denounce rising living costs and growing inequality.
The atmosphere deteriorated sharply after the rally ended. Riot police fired tear gas and water cannon at a group of around 500 hooded youths before they eventually dispersed on a cold, rainy evening.
In France’s second city, Marseille, youths set fire to rubbish bins to block roads, and hurled rocks and bottles at security forces. Police said several stores, including two jewellery shops, were ransacked.
Clashes also flared in Lyon, Bordeaux, Grenoble, Clermont-Ferrand, Lille, Rennes, Nantes and Toulouse.
"In almost every march we saw the formation of these high-risk groups. They broke away from the main body and sought to commit acts of violence," said Interior Minister Laurent Nunez, accusing far-left activists and criminal gangs of seeking to foment trouble.
PARIS IN LOCKDOWN
Authorities deployed 70,000 police officers and gendarmes, 10,000 more than a week earlier, after conceding they had underestimated the scale of the unrest on October 17.
Nunez told reporters the violence was less intense than a week ago, when looters and vandals went on the rampage. "What changed was anticipation," he said.
He also said far-right activists had sought confrontations with leftist groups in the southern cities of Nice and Montpellier, opening a potential new front in the disturbances.
Much of central Paris took on the appearance of a city under lockdown, with shopkeepers boarding up storefronts, museums closing their doors and more than 20 metro stations shut.
Business groups urged retailers to remain closed after thousands of shops and businesses were damaged or looted across France last weekend.
"There are hardly any customers, so it’s not really worth staying open," said Oskar, manager of a Kiton boutique in Paris.
Several of the capital’s best-known cultural institutions, including the Louvre, the Musee d’Orsay and the Paris Opera, closed for the day as a precaution, leaving tourists frustrated.
"Everything’s boarded up and we’re not quite sure where we should be," said Xavier Dolliole, a tourist from the US city of New Orleans.
PROTESTS RIPPLE ACROSS EUROPE
The nationwide disorder began with small student demonstrations in suburban Paris last month to denounce school conditions. It swiftly broadened into a wider protest against the government’s economic policies and inspired demonstrations in neighbouring countries.
On Saturday Belgian police used tear gas and pepper spray as they clashed in Brussels with anti-government demonstrators, with protests also taking place in a number of Italian cities for a second weekend, and in Albania.
Hard-left leader Jean-Luc Melenchon, who joined the Paris rally, predicted the protests would continue until President Emmanuel Macron, whose mandate expires next year, addressed the social malaise in France, one of the world’s richest nations.
"Given the current situation, I think he will come to understand that this will happen again every week. There is still time for (Macron) to give in. After that, the only thing left to him will be the exit door," Melenchon told reporters.
FAR-RIGHT PARTY HOLDS CONGRESS
Many demonstrators accused the government of overreacting to last week’s turmoil, as soldiers were dispatched to patrol the Champs-Elysees, a grand boulevard lined with luxury shops and restaurants.
"We shed tears for shops, not for the people who are being impoverished all year round," said Clara Lebbadi, a 22-year-old arts student.
"My friend and I almost didn’t come because we were scared, but we came precisely because it’s important not to let repression win," she added.
The first authorised march on Saturday passed off peacefully in Orléans, around 120 km (75 miles) south of Paris, where demonstrators rallied against Marine Le Pen’s far-right National Rally, which is holding a party congress in the city.
A shooting west of Paris on Friday heightened tensions. A gunman suspected of acting out of Islamophobic hatred killed one person and wounded four others, including a 12-year-old girl.
"We have come to tell the far right, face-to-face, that we are not afraid," said Bally Bagayoko, the mayor of Saint-Denis and a member of Melenchon’s France Unbowed party.

Their plan faces a reckoning on Sunday, when Senator Flavio Bolsonaro faces leftist President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva in a tight run-off. Lula has warned Washington against encroaching on Brazil’s sovereignty and accused his opponent of plotting with the Trump administration.
The two officials were Darren Beattie, a Senior Advisor for Western Hemisphere Affairs who oversees Brazil policy, and Ricardo Pita, another senior advisor promoted this year to Deputy Assistant Secretary for North America. The details of their campaign to return the Bolsonaros to power haven’t been previously reported.
Beattie and Pita, both political appointees, operated with wide latitude to manage Washington’s relationship with the second most-populous country in the Americas, the people said.
In the months before election campaigning began, they instructed US diplomats in Brazil that it was US policy to restore former President Jair Bolsonaro as Brazil’s leader – even though he had been disqualified from office for plotting a coup in 2022, when he lost the presidential election to Lula, three of the people said.
After Bolsonaro received a 27-year sentence in September 2025, the two men pivoted to supporting the candidacy of his son, right-wing Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, the three sources said. Beattie and Pita told embassy staff not to interact with other conservative presidential contenders who could challenge the younger Bolsonaro, they said.
Since last year, the two men have successfully advocated for punitive US government measures on Brazil designed to weaken Lula and boost the Bolsonaros, the 10 people told Reuters. The policies included designating Brazilian gangs as terrorist groups and imposing US sanctions against the Brazilian Supreme Court Justice who was spearheading the investigation into Jair Bolsonaro.
Reuters could not determine the extent to which the two men were acting on orders from the White House or Secretary of State Marco Rubio. Trump, a vocal defender of Bolsonaro since his election defeat in 2022, hasn’t publicly endorsed any candidate.
The White House declined to comment and referred questions to the State Department.
State Department Spokesman Tommy Pigott didn’t answer questions about specific measures and directives involving Beattie and Pita but said in a statement: "All actions taken by the United States against narco-traffickers and to protect free speech are to defend the rights and lives of the American people. The Brazilian people have the right to choose their leaders through free and fair elections."
Lula’s office did not respond to comment requests.
Orna Blum, one of the officials who spoke to Reuters about Beattie and Pita’s efforts, led the State Department’s Brazil and Southern Cone office until retiring last year over her opposition to the Trump administration.
Washington "has every right to pursue its economic and strategic interests," she said. "But when American foreign policy instruments are used to pressure another democracy over the legal fate of a political ally, the line between diplomacy and political intervention has been crossed."
SANCTIONS ON A SUPREME COURT JUSTICE
Beattie is a former White House speechwriter fired in 2018 after addressing an event frequented by white nationalists. He’s also the architect of "free speech diplomacy," a policy advocated by Trump allies that seeks to punish nations they accuse of censoring right-wing speech by US citizens, companies and global right-wing allies.
The United States has accused Brazil Supreme Court Justice Alexandre de Moraes of violating free speech rights by jailing Brazilians for political social-media posts and by censoring content of US social-media companies. Moraes has argued he was ridding social media of fake news that undermined public faith in Brazil’s democratic institutions.
Moraes did not respond to a comment request.
Pita, a conservative Venezuelan-American, is among many in Rubio’s orbit who view Lula as a threat to US interests in Latin America. Rubio has been a key leader in the administration’s aggressive policy in the region, which has included an invasion of Venezuela to oust its president, an oil blockade of Cuba, and military attacks on suspected drug boats from Latin America.
Beattie and Pita were drawn to the Bolsonaro family’s right-wing politics, their antipathy towards Lula, and the idea that Jair Bolsonaro was a victim of abuses by Brazil’s Supreme Court.
Like Trump in the 2020 US election, Bolsonaro refused to concede he lost Brazil’s 2022 presidential vote, triggering riots by supporters who stormed government buildings. The Supreme Court convicted him in September 2025 of plotting a coup to remain in power.
Before the conviction, in early 2025, the Bolsonaros were aggressively lobbying Washington for sanctions under the Global Magnitsky Human Rights Accountability Act against Moraes, who had led criminal investigations into Jair Bolsonaro. The act is a 2016 federal law allowing US sanctions against foreign individuals responsible for human-rights abuses or severe corruption.
Around April 2025, Jair Bolsonaro’s younger son, Eduardo, visited Beattie in his State Department office in Washington DC, according to two former US officials. Eduardo Bolsonaro had been making the public case for Magnitsky sanctions against Moraes since at least 2024, and in March 2025 he said in a livestream that it was "practically certain" the Trump administration would do so.
Eduardo Bolsonaro did not respond to requests for comment.
Beattie made calls to the US Treasury Department’s Office of Foreign Assets Control to appeal for Magnitsky sanctions against Moraes, said a former US official with direct knowledge of the matter.
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, whose department administers Magnitsky sanctions through OFAC, offered no opposition, the former official said.
The US announced Magnitsky sanctions against Moraes in July 2025, citing his alleged violations of free-speech rights by censoring anti-government social-media posts.
A Treasury official said Bessent and Rubio are "fully aligned on the administration’s foreign policy."
TERRORIST DESIGNATIONS
The Bolsonaro family was also pushing for Washington to designate Brazil’s top gangs – the Primeiro Comando da Capital (PCC) and Comando Vermelho (CV) – as terrorist organizations. They believed such a designation would hurt Lula, who some opponents have criticized for failing to control crime.
Eduardo Bolsonaro had become friends with Pita through US conservative circles, and both supported the effort to designate the gangs as terrorist groups.
In May 2025, Pita joined a US delegation that visited Jair Bolsonaro at his residence in Brasilia as he awaited his trial, according to public announcements at the time. Also in the group: David Gamble, the State Department’s top sanctions official at the time.
Back in Washington, Pita asked State sanctions officials to explore how terrorist designations like those announced against Mexican cartels in February 2025 could be used in Brazil, one former official said.
Nearly a year later, in May 2026 – after Pita was promoted to a new job that pulled him out of Brazil affairs – presidential contender Flavio Bolsonaro met with Beattie and Deputy Secretary of State Christopher Landau in Washington to discuss "the urgency of designating the PCC and the Comando Vermelho as foreign terrorist organizations," according to an X post by right-wing influencer Paulo Figueiredo that included photos of the attendees.
The State Department announced the designation the following day.
Reuters could not determine the extent of Pita or Beattie’s influence in securing the final decision.
BACKFIRES AND SETBACKS
In July 2025, Washington also announced a series of other measures against Brazil, including the revocations of eight Supreme Court justices’ visas and 50% tariffs on Brazilian goods, citing the "persecution" of Jair Bolsonaro.
Reuters could not determine what, if any, role Beattie or Pita played in the additional measures. But if they were intended to undermine Lula, many of them backfired, according to political analysts in Brazil.
Measures targeting the court did nothing to stop it from proceeding with Bolsonaro’s trial, while the tariffs boosted the Lula government’s poll numbers, the analysts said.
Major US and Brazilian firms reliant on bilateral trade – including meatpacking giant JBS - controlled by Brazilian billionaires Wesley and Joesley Batista – also pushed back on the tariffs, which Washington eventually watered down.
Beattie and Pita’s campaign also hit setbacks. Without an official explanation from the Treasury Department, the US removed Justice Moraes from the Magnitsky sanctions list in December, and in March Brazil barred Beattie from entering the country to visit Bolsonaro in prison.
Mario Braga, a Latin America analyst at risk intelligence firm RANE, said Trump may have decided to withhold a public endorsement of Bolsonaro to avoid being seen as meddling in Brazil’s election – a perception that could boost Lula’s popularity.
Still, after Flavio Bolsonaro narrowly outperformed Lula in the first-round election earlier this month, Trump called it a big victory.
"Close, but a very, very big victory," he told reporters. "Amazing, actually."

title: Policy choices will matter crucially amid growing socioeconomic challenges
full_text:
Investing.com - Rapid population ageing and declining birth rates are threatening to shave up to 2 percentage points off global economic growth while driving pension and healthcare costs up by at least 5% of GDP across developed economies by 2060, according to a research report from UBS Global Research.
In a report examining global demographic trends, UBS economist Reinhard Cluse warned that demographic change has evolved from concerns over overpopulation into an era of "depopulation" that will reshape public balance sheets, labour supply, and capital markets.
"Alongside climate change, artificial intelligence, geopolitical fragmentation and rising public debt, demographic change will be one of the defining megatrends of the decades ahead," Cluse wrote.
Fertility collapse and population contractions
Global fertility rates have dropped from around 5 children per woman in the early 1960s to approximately 2.25 today, with more than half of all nations - accounting for two-thirds of the world’s population - falling below the replacement threshold of 2.1.
The United Nations projects the world population will peak at roughly 10.3 billion in the mid-2080s before contracting. However, national demographic paths are sharply diverging.
Sixty-three countries - representing 28% of global population, including China, Germany, Japan, Italy, and South Korea - have already passed peak population. China’s population is projected to drop by 54% from 1.4 billion today to 649 million by 2100.
Forty-eight countries, including Brazil, Vietnam, and Turkey, are expected to reach peak population within the next 30 years.
Africa is projected to see its share of the world population surge from 19% today to 37% by 2100, driven by younger age structures in countries such as Nigeria, Ethiopia, and the Democratic Republic of the Congo.
Macroeconomic drag and fiscal strains
Citing International Monetary Fund estimates, UBS noted that demographic ageing is set to reduce global annual GDP growth by 1.1 percentage points over 2025–2050 compared to 2016–2018 baselines, and by 2 percentage points on average over 2025-2100.
The growth deceleration stems primarily from contracting labour forces, lower domestic capital formation, and slowing productivity gains. UBS emphasized that the retirement of the baby-boomer generation is not a temporary shock; persistently low birth rates mean old-age dependency ratios will stabilize at permanently higher levels.
The fiscal fallout poses acute risks for sovereign debt sustainability. In OECD countries, public outlays on pensions, healthcare, and long-term care are projected to rise from an average of 16.7% of GDP to over 21.6% by 2060. At the same time, shrinking workforces threaten to erode income tax and social security receipts.
Policy dilemma: The ’ageing paradox’
UBS highlighted what it termed an "ageing paradox": while demographic decline escalates the necessity for structural reforms - such as lifting statutory retirement ages, broadening tax bases, and encouraging technological innovation - an older median electorate tends to resist welfare retrenchment and public investment in favor of preserving entitlements.
While artificial intelligence adoption could lift productivity and ease labour constraints, UBS cautioned that AI is unlikely to serve as a complete cure. Ageing shifts aggregate consumer demand toward personal services like healthcare and elder care, sectors where automation and productivity gains remain difficult to achieve.
Furthermore, while sustained immigration can cushion demographic deficits in countries like the United States, Canada, and the UK, UBS referenced the "demographic trilemma," arguing that ageing nations with ultra-low fertility will struggle to simultaneously maintain economic dynamism and ethnic homogeneity without significant political friction.

title: Volkswagen to build Georgia Audi plant, expand in SC - Bloomberg
full_text:
Investing.com - Volkswagen AG will build a new manufacturing facility for its luxury Audi brand in Georgia and expand an assembly plant in South Carolina, U.S. President Donald Trump is set to announce Saturday, Bloomberg News reported.
The German automaker is pursuing the multi-site U.S. manufacturing expansion in hopes of securing relief from import tariffs that have weighed heavily on company earnings, a U.S. official familiar with the negotiations told Bloomberg.
Under the plan, Volkswagen will construct a greenfield factory in Macon, Georgia, dedicated to producing Audi Q7, Q8, and Q9 sport-utility vehicles, according to the official, who spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss private deliberations. The Macon plant is slated to begin construction shortly and will feature an annual production capacity of 200,000 vehicles.
Concurrently, Volkswagen will expand its Scout Motors electric vehicle plant currently under construction in Blythewood, South Carolina, adding 25,000 units of annual capacity for an undetermined vehicle line.
Trump plans to unveil the industrial investment Saturday evening during a campaign rally in Perry, Georgia—near the planned Macon site—as the administration seeks to highlight domestic manufacturing gains ahead of the Nov. 3 midterm elections, where several key Republican candidates face tight races.
In exchange for the investments, the administration and Volkswagen will continue discussions regarding tariff adjustments. Any policy relief would extend industry-wide rather than benefit Volkswagen exclusively, the official noted.
Negotiations are centered on a framework that would award proportional tariff credits to automakers that commit capital to establishing or expanding production footprints within the United States.

title: Can silver recover from its latest sell-off? UBS weighs in
full_text:
Investing.com - Silver faces near-term turbulence as central banks maintain monetary policy pressure, but prices are poised to reach $80 an ounce by late 2027 amid expanding artificial intelligence infrastructure demand and persistent structural supply deficits, according to a research note from UBS Global Wealth Management.
In a report published by the bank’s Chief Investment Office, UBS strategist Giovanni Staunovo noted that while silver has come under renewed selling pressure, the medium-term backdrop remains constructive as the white metal continues to track gold as a higher-beta asset.
UBS targets silver rising from a spot price of $55.90 an ounce on Oct. 22 to $70.00 by December 2026, climbing to $75.00 through mid-2027 and reaching $80.00 by September 2027.
"Silver continues to behave like a higher-beta version of gold, benefiting, and suffering, from many of the same macro forces," Staunovo wrote, warning that shifts in real interest rates, U.S. dollar strength, and monetary tightening will continue to trigger sharp price swings.
AI and automotive demand counter solar thrifting
Industrial fundamentals for silver are diverging across end-markets. Elevated prices have accelerated substitution and thrifting, particularly within the photovoltaic solar sector, prompting the Silver Institute to forecast an approximate 2% contraction in total industrial fabrication demand for 2026.
However, that drag is being counterbalanced by secular growth across data center expansion, AI hardware, electrical grid investments, and automotive electronics.
On the supply side, secondary recycling flows have increased in reaction to higher market prices, but overall mine output growth remains rigid. Because the vast majority of silver is extracted as a byproduct of lead, zinc, copper, and gold mining operations, miners face structural constraints in rapidly ramping up output to capitalize on elevated price levels.
As a result, UBS projects the global silver market will record its sixth consecutive annual deficit in 2026.
Rather than chasing price rallies, UBS advises investors to adopt a selective strategy, using pullbacks driven by interest rate expectations to build exposure. The bank identified prolonged central bank rate hikes, a sharper global economic slowdown, and faster industrial substitution as the primary downside risks to its price trajectory.
